analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare hospitals and surgery centers to publish their prices for at least 300 common services.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote in either House committee and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require hospitals and ambulatory surgical centers that take Medicare to publicly post their standard charges, discounted cash prices, and pricing for at least 300 'shoppable services' — things like MRIs, colonoscopies, and joint replacements that patients can schedule in advance and compare across facilities. Facilities that don't comply could face federal fines of up to $2 million a year. The bill was introduced by Rep. Michelle Steel in July 2023, sent to two House committees, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients — including uninsured people paying cash and people with high-deductible insurance — who could see a hospital's actual price for a service before getting it, and shop across facilities. Employers, insurers, and researchers could also use the published data to compare hospital prices.

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals and ambulatory surgical centers must publish, free of charge, lists of standard charges, discounted cash prices, and prices for at least 300 shoppable services that patients can schedule in advance [S2][S3].
Hospitals must also post a consumer-friendly price estimator tool that gives an immediate estimate without requiring an account, so a patient can see a price before agreeing to care [S3].

Facilities that fail to comply face daily civil monetary penalties, up to $2 million per year for larger hospitals, and noncompliant hospitals would be flagged publicly on the Medicare Hospital Compare website [S3].
The bill gives CMS $10 million to enforce the requirements and requires HHS to publish which hospitals were penalized and whether they came into compliance [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and ambulatory surgical centers, which bear the cost of compiling and publishing prices, updating websites, and potential fines. Taxpayers fund the $10 million implementation appropriation. Patients would eventually benefit if disclosure pressures prices down, but publication alone does not guarantee that.

drawbacks.text: Publishing prices does not itself lower them. A hospital can post prices truthfully and keep them high; patients in emergencies or rural areas with only one nearby hospital cannot shop on price at all.

Hospitals with a qualifying price estimator tool are deemed compliant with the shoppable-services requirement, which lets them satisfy part of the mandate through their own website tools rather than standardized public data files [S3].
The bill adds administrative work for thousands of facilities, and CMS must spend $10 million in a single year building compliance monitoring and public reporting systems [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit is real but modest: patients could look up what a hospital charges for a scheduled procedure before agreeing to it, and the biggest ones face fines up to $2 million a year for hiding it. The costs are compliance work for hospitals, $10 million in federal implementation funding, and the honest caveat that transparency alone rarely forces prices down without enforcement and consumer use. A well-designed, low-cost consumer protection that was never tested by a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees — and later in their Health Subcommittee — from July 2023 until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, never receiving a markup or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Michelle Steel introduced the bill on July 24, 2023, and it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee [S1][S5].
It was referred to the Health Subcommittee in July 2023 and again in December 2024, but neither committee ever took it up [S5].
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and ambulatory surgical centers are better off because the bill died: they avoided new disclosure duties, compliance costs, and penalties of up to $2 million a year. No patient or consumer group gained anything from the outcome.

sides.party_line_note: There is no vote or cosponsor record to show a partisan split: the sponsor was a Republican, no member of either party signed on, and no committee or floor vote ever occurred [S4][S5].

industries.note: Hospitals would have had to publish full chargemaster charges, discounted cash prices, and pricing for at least 300 shoppable services, flag noncompliance on the public Hospital Compare site, and face daily fines up to $2 million a year for larger facilities. Public disclosure of prices undermines hospitals' ability to keep charge differences opaque across patients and payers [S3].
Surgery centers would face the same disclosure duties starting in 2028, including cash prices for 300 shoppable services and penalties up to $300 per day [S3].

The bill lets, but does not require, hospitals to publish payer-specific negotiated rates; if widely disclosed, insurers' negotiated prices would become publicly comparable. Insurers also benefit indirectly if hospital transparency gives their members usable price estimates [S3].
